name: human
description: How to communicate clearly with Gilad — the human leader. Read this reference when your leader is Gilad, on top of the ai-to-leader base skill.
---
You are **conversing with a human.**

<adhd>
I have ADHD. I am cognitively overloaded in my day-to-day. It manifests as (a) forgetfulness, and (b) difficulty taking in long and dense texts.

<adhd.forgetfulness>
This increases forgetfulness.
My forgetfulness isn’t deletion of memory — my memory persists and consolidates well — it’s difficulty to retrieve memories that were active only once or twice, where last time was 1–2 days ago (or more). It’s like my brain cleared up cached context and needs to load it again. The remedy is to recall: successful recall of a vague memory makes it easier to retrieve it next time, as the memory gradually becomes a reflex.

<adhd.forgetfulness.mitigation>
Help me recall.
I don’t need much to be able to recall a vague-but-recent memory — just a bit of wider context, the motivation behind the work, and latest progress, devoid of tiny details, all in short, simple, linear sentences. Aim for me to have a “Oh right, of course! yes, good, let’s resume” moment.
</adhd.forgetfulness.mitigation>
</adhd.forgetfulness>

<adhd.how-it-shows-up-in-daily-life>
Concretely: I juggle many different AI coding sessions in parallel (hits ‘b’). Many project-scoped sessions can be active across multiple days (hits ‘a’).
Practically: if I tell you I’m vague on what we’ve been doing, recall this `adhd` section and apply `adhd.forgetfulness.mitigation`. 

<adhd.how-it-shows-up-in-daily-life.apply-asd-ste100>
Always use ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English when you talk to me.

**WORDS:**
- **Use one name for one thing. Do not reference a thing in multiple ways. Do not call the same item by two different names.** Applies throughout whole conversations and project histories, not just one message: Keep using the one name the thing has had since as far back as you can tell. Just like it is better to reuse a single variable holding some value.
- Use the short common word: start (not begin/commence/initiate), use (not utilize/leverage), help (not facilitate), make sure (not ensure), before (not prior to), after (not subsequent to), about (not regarding/concerning), get (not obtain/acquire), show (not demonstrate), also (not additionally/furthermore/moreover).
- Give each word one meaning. "fall" means to move down, not to decrease.
- No marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, powerful, cutting-edge, effortless, world-class, next-generation, revolutionary.
- No flair.

**VERBS:**
- Active voice. "the parser reads the file", not "the file is read by the parser".
- Use a verb for an action. "analyze the log", not "perform an analysis of the log".
- No stacked auxiliaries. Not "it is important to note that this may help to improve". Write "this improves X".
- No "-ing" main verb where a simple tense works.

**SENTENCES:**
- One instruction per sentence. Max 20 words (instruction), max 25 (descriptive).
- No contractions. Use articles: a, an, the, this, these.

**PUNCTUATION:**
- No semicolons nor em dashes. Write two sentences.

**STRUCTURE:**
- One topic per paragraph. Max six sentences, preferrably 3–4. For steps, use a numbered vertical list, one action per item, imperative form. Put a condition before its command.
- Write only the requested text. No preamble, no summary, no closing remarks.
- No interlocked look-behind and look-ahead references. Write linearly.
</adhd.how-it-shows-up-in-daily-life.apply-asd-ste100>
</adhd.how-it-shows-up-in-daily-life>

<adhd.required-writing-style>
- Write clear, succinct, **rich and eye-pleasing Markdown prose.** Keep it well-written, simple and well-styled, no fluff, and **not verbose**. Brightly communicate what you mean, with enough context to be useful, but no more than enough. Recall “The Elements of Style”.
- Do not force content into a list when prose would work better; descriptions and opinions read better as well-shaped paragraphs. Use a list when the material naturally breaks into distinct, scannable items or when the items build on one another, such as steps, tasks, requirements, options, processes, timelines, lines of reasoning, or examples.
- When a list is the right shape, use a numbered list by default. Use bullets only for genuinely unordered peer items, where numbers would falsely imply sequence, priority, or progression.

<adhd.required-writing-style.behavior>
- Say **why** you did the thing.
- **Do not** flag concerns unless something materially affects **risk, product/business human decisions, or current work’s scope in an important way**; otherwise do not spend the human’s attention on caveats.
- **Be precise about uncertainty**: “I am not sure this library supports streaming” tells the human what to verify; “I think this should work” does not.
{# following bullets should probably be moved to the engineering tenets part #}
- **Done means done.** Not half done. Not done except for the part you decided to skip. And not a report about how it will be done.
{# - Five things asked means five things delivered, no matter how long they'll take. If the fifth is genuinely blocked, finish the other four and name the blocker in one sentence. The specific blocker. Not "this needs more investigation." #}
</adhd.required-writing-style.behavior>

<adhd.required-writing-style.work-summaries>
- Your final summary for the human is a specific event. You have to keep in mind the following: **Your post-work summary is for a reader who didn’t see any of your work, haven’t read any of your interim step-summaries, and definitely was not there with you in the trenches of implementation and managing your own delegates.**
- Read `theory-of-mind.md`. Truly read it now. It is always relevant. Your human-facing work summary is that situation, asymmetry by absence: the human was not with you while you worked, and your final message is their first look and their entry point to your work. **Write it as a re-grounding:** the outcome first.
- If you need to escalate something to the human, explain it as if new.
- When you write the summary at the end, **drop the working shorthand, drop the internal lingo.** This is the best opportunity to apply ASD-STE100-flavored easy-to-read Markdown prose.
- Drop details that don’t change what the human would do next.
</adhd.required-writing-style.work-summaries>
</adhd.required-writing-style>
</adhd>

Sender: /root/simple_team_audit
Payload:
Read all four root Markdown docs, runtime, registry, child callbacks, dashboard, renderers, and render support. No repository changes or model calls.

**Simple-team has real retention defects, but none yet explains the observed Herdr slowdown.**

1. **RPC stderr grows without a limit.** [index.ts:419](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/index.ts:419) appends every stderr chunk to `teammate.stderr`. Nothing reads or clears that buffer. It survives until the team leaves memory, including teammate restarts within the same team. This is a definite unnecessary retention path. Its impact requires substantial stderr traffic.

2. **Animated pending calls leak tool contexts and repeated invalidations.** [text.ts:129](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/render-support/text.ts:129) stores contexts in a module-level map. [text.ts:183](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/render-support/text.ts:183) returns immediately for completed calls, before cleanup. Result renderers never call `clearBlink`. A no-model probe confirmed two invalidations during 950ms **after completion**. This requires `pendingStatusAnimation=true`. The default is false, and the global settings contain no explicit setting. Treat it as a confirmed conditional defect, not confirmed attribution.

3. **Resize work grows with transcript size.** Each `TeamLines` width change calls `stableRenderWidth`, which synchronously discovers settings files, reads settings, and parses JSON. See [render.ts:115](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/render.ts:115), [ansi.ts:49](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/render-support/ansi.ts:49), and [settings.ts:72](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/render-support/settings.ts:72). A scratch benchmark of 1,000 tiny views across ten width changes took 415ms, approximately 41ms per resize. This measures the full renderer, not settings overhead alone. It depends on retained transcript views, not elapsed time.

4. **The team log is bounded by count, but not bytes.** [teamlog.ts:138](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/teamlog.ts:138) retains 1,000 entries per live team. Tool entries retain complete arguments and results, including potential image content, at [teamlog.ts:272](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/teamlog.ts:272). Several large results can consume substantial parent memory. This reaches a rolling limit for stable payload sizes. It is not indefinite growth per event.

5. **Idle teammates remain real processes by design.** They stop through `team_shutdown` or parent `session_shutdown`. Restarting the same visible sessions does not automatically restore these RPC processes. Therefore, the restart comparison does **not** hold background process count constant. This is an important confound.

Counterevidence:

- `shutdownTeam` removes its team from the module map at [index.ts:609](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/index.ts:609).
- Reminder timers delete themselves after firing and clear during shutdown.
- The dashboard timer clears on close/disposal at [team-ui.ts:242](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/team-ui.ts:242).
- The dashboard renders all retained message/log entries before clipping. That costs CPU, but only while the overlay is open.
- Renderer caches retain only one width, not every width encountered.
- RPC stdout is ignored at [index.ts:411](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/index.ts:411). It does not accumulate a parent-side RPC transcript.

A weaker conditional concern: child lifecycle callbacks queue complete tool results and turn messages before HTTP delivery. Slow callbacks can retain queued payloads. Normal successful delivery drains the queue. I found no evidence of a persistent backlog.

Payload:
**Herdr scrollback is a strong independent suspect. The reboot evidence does not isolate Pi or either extension.**

1. **Native Pi restore discards Herdr’s old terminal history.** Even with `pane_history=true`, a native agent restore sets `initial_history_ansi=None`. Herdr expects Pi to redraw its conversation. See [restore.rs:739](/tmp/herdr-resize-investigation/src/persist/restore.rs:739) and [restore.rs:774](/tmp/herdr-resize-investigation/src/persist/restore.rs:774). Existing tests cover Pi and assert history suppression at lines 1081 and 1107. Consequently, identical Pi JSONL files can coexist with much smaller Herdr scrollback after restart.

2. **Width changes reflow retained terminal rows synchronously.** [pane.rs:2609](/tmp/herdr-resize-investigation/src/pane.rs:2609) skips unchanged dimensions, then immediately resizes the terminal. [terminal.rs:1576](/tmp/herdr-resize-investigation/src/pane/terminal.rs:1576) holds the terminal lock during resize. Ghostty’s [PageList.zig:1225](/tmp/herdr-resize-investigation/vendor/libghostty-vt/src/terminal/PageList.zig:1225) states that resize decompresses all nodes. [PageList.zig:1410](/tmp/herdr-resize-investigation/vendor/libghostty-vt/src/terminal/PageList.zig:1410) reflows all rows. Primary-screen resize enables reflow with wraparound at [Terminal.zig:3557](/tmp/herdr-resize-investigation/vendor/libghostty-vt/src/terminal/Terminal.zig:3557).

3. **Sidebar changes can multiply this across hidden panes.** Desktop view computation calls background-pane resizing at [ui.rs:290](/tmp/herdr-resize-investigation/src/ui.rs:290). [ui.rs:174](/tmp/herdr-resize-investigation/src/ui.rs:174) walks other workspaces and tabs. A split-border drag primarily changes its affected panes; unchanged-size checks protect other panes.

4. **Retained history is bounded, but its processing can still become expensive.** Default scrollback is 10,000,000 bytes per pane at [config.rs:53](/tmp/herdr-resize-investigation/src/config.rs:53). Ordinary history snapshots request all retained history through `usize::MAX`, [pane.rs:2788](/tmp/herdr-resize-investigation/src/pane.rs:2788). I found no separate restore truncation. Native Pi restore instead suppresses that history completely.

5. **`pane_history=true` adds another synchronous cost.** [session.rs:72](/tmp/herdr-resize-investigation/src/app/session.rs:72) captures the save job before starting its background thread. Capture collects every pane’s history at lines 53–54. The background thread only performs serialization/write work after capture. This can cause pauses when a session save follows layout changes, although I did not trace every dirty-state trigger.

Graphics inspection found explicit cleanup for replaced images and removed pane layers. Terminal image metadata can outlive visible placements, but I did not establish a leak or its relevance here.

The checkout is exactly v0.8.2, commit `9eb521456ac0d19d3ab3d9d7cea3cca10baa8a4c`, dated August 19. The pre-reboot running binary version remains unknown. No benchmark or live manipulation performed.

**Scope-limited conclusion:** accumulated Herdr terminal scrollback explains resize-specific slowdown and restart recovery without requiring any memory leak. A CPU sample during recurrence should distinguish Ghostty reflow/history capture from Pi rendering or memory pressure.

Message Type: FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: /root
Sender: /root/other_extensions_audit
Payload:
Other extensions remain plausible contributors. I found **two concrete redraw costs**, but no proven large memory leak.

1. **Timestamp adds transient transcript components throughout use.**  
   [timestamp.ts:218](/Users/giladbarnea/.pi/agent/npm/node_modules/@hk_net/pi-timestamp/timestamp.ts:218) calls `ctx.ui.notify` for each user message. The settled-run handler adds another notification. These notifications do not persist in the session file. If Pi retains notification components in its chat container, restarting removes accumulated components while restoring the same conversation. This fits the reboot evidence better than ordinary message-count cost. Parent should connect this to Pi’s notification implementation.

2. **Custom footer scans the complete session branch on every render.**  
   [custom-footer/index.ts:426](/Users/giladbarnea/.pi/agent/extensions/custom-footer/index.ts:426) calls `getSessionStats`. Its loop at line 307 scans `getBranch()`, including history before compaction. Resize therefore adds work proportional to branch length. It also writes status changes synchronously to disk at line 575. This is definite repeated work, but not evidence of retention. Restoring the same branch should restore this cost.

3. **Pretty Bash adds repeated rendering work, but its wrappers do not accumulate.**  
   [pi-pretty-bash/index.ts:94](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-pretty-bash/index.ts:94) runs `truncateToVisualLines` on highlighted JSON every render, without a width cache. Each result retains original and highlighted strings. I checked upstream: [renderers/bash.js:36](/opt/homebrew/lib/node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/dist/core/tools/renderers/bash.js:36) clears and recreates children before wrapping. Therefore, repeated result updates do not stack wrappers. This cost also returns after session restoration.

4. **Current pi-subagents has explicit retention limits.**  
   [agent-manager.ts:1470](/Users/giladbarnea/.pi/agent/npm/node_modules/@tintinweb/pi-subagents/src/agent-manager.ts:1470) evicts completed sessions after ten minutes. The cleanup timer runs every minute. Tombstones cap at 100. Child disposal explicitly emits shutdown at line 339. This reduces suspicion of permanently retained completed children in the current installed version. I did not establish what version ran before reboot.

5. **Two Moshi integrations are enabled.**  
   Both `extensions/moshi-hooks.ts` and `extensions/moshi-hooks/index.ts` dispatch detached helper processes for session and agent events. Neither sets a timeout. The older directory version sends the whole `agent_end` event, including messages. This can duplicate process and serialization work. The current process snapshot showed one Moshi daemon, not a buildup of helper processes.

`pi list` ran successfully. Its `(filtered)` label means a package has resource filters, **not that it is disabled**. Explicitly enabled packages include todo, subagents, fff, MCP adapter, timestamp, and plannotator. Local auto-discovery also includes unlisted extensions such as `herdr-agent-state.ts`.

The herdr integration coalesces state updates into one pending slot and destroys sockets after bounded attempts. Time Sense has no periodic timer. Context heads-up stores only scalar state. Wasted Read stores path hashes and clears them on session start, compaction, and tree changes.

Limits: static source audit and one process snapshot only. I did not execute extension hooks or resolve resources through a loader that might start external services. Current settings do not prove what every existing Pi process loaded. No files or live sessions changed.

text(await tools.exec_command({cmd:"cat > diagnostics/2026-09-05/findings.md <<'EOF'
# Restart recovery points to accumulated runtime state, not necessarily a leak

The reported slowdown affects herdr sidebar changes, pane creation/removal, and border dragging after roughly two weeks. A computer restart followed by restoration of the same workspaces, tabs, panes, and AI sessions made these actions much faster.

That is strong evidence against saved conversation size being the sole cause. It does not identify which process accumulated the expensive state. Restoring the same conversation does not restore the same terminal scrollback, child processes, widget rows, or transient notifications.

**No measured leak has yet been tied to the reported slowdown. Herdr terminal scrollback is the strongest structural match found in this audit.** There are also concrete extension costs and retention defects.

## Herdr discards old terminal scrollback when it resumes Pi

Herdr v0.8.2 native agent restore sets `initial_history_ansi` to `None`, even when `pane_history=true`. Pi redraws its saved conversation instead. Thus, identical Pi session files after reboot do not imply identical herdr terminal history. [Restore implementation](https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr/blob/9eb521456ac0d19d3ab3d9d7cea3cca10baa8a4c/src/persist/restore.rs#L739).

Width changes synchronously resize the terminal while holding its lock. Ghostty resize decompresses retained nodes and reflows retained rows. Desktop layout changes can resize panes in background tabs and workspaces too. Unchanged-size checks skip unaffected panes. This makes accumulated terminal history relevant to sidebar changes across a large workspace setup. [Pane resize](https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr/blob/9eb521456ac0d19d3ab3d9d7cea3cca10baa8a4c/src/pane.rs#L2609), [background pane resize](https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr/blob/9eb521456ac0d19d3ab3d9d7cea3cca10baa8a4c/src/ui.rs#L174), [Ghostty reflow](https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr/blob/9eb521456ac0d19d3ab3d9d7cea3cca10baa8a4c/vendor/libghostty-vt/src/terminal/PageList.zig#L1225).

The default scrollback budget is 10,000,000 bytes per pane. Bounded history can still become expensive to reflow. The local configuration enables `pane_history` and `kitty_graphics`. History capture also occurs synchronously before the save worker starts. This is another possible pause source, although the audit did not prove which reported actions trigger a save. [History capture](https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr/blob/9eb521456ac0d19d3ab3d9d7cea3cca10baa8a4c/src/app/session.rs#L53).

This remains a source-backed hypothesis. There is no CPU profile from the slow, pre-reboot state. Fullscreen/alternate-screen behavior affects how much primary scrollback actually accumulated.

## Pi and the extensions add distinct costs

Pi is the interactive coding-agent CLI. Its SDK exposes the same agent/session machinery inside another program. `pi-user-agents` creates SDK child sessions inside the parent Pi process. `pi-simple-team` creates separate RPC Pi processes. Their memory must therefore be attributed differently.

| Component | Finding | Fit with restart recovery |
|---|---|---|
| `pi-user-agents` | A widget with only idle agents still requests rendering every 100 ms. Each preview builds fresh Markdown from the full response before truncation. | Widget rows and their timer disappear on session restart. This can remove substantial CPU work. |
| `pi-user-agents` | Live child histories, inherited snapshots, fingerprints, and completed child snapshots remain in memory while their rows remain. | Restart removes these live objects. This is largely intentional retention, not proof of unreachable-object leakage. |
| `pi-user-agents` | Every result card stores the complete selected child exchange up to that turn. Total stored card content grows quadratically with follow-up count. | The cards persist, so this alone does not explain recovery with the same file. |
| `pi-simple-team` | RPC stderr appends indefinitely to an unused string. | A concrete unnecessary retention path. Its impact depends on actual stderr volume. |
| `pi-simple-team` | Optional pending-call animation retains completed tool contexts and continues invalidation. | Confirmed defect, but the option defaults to false and is absent from global settings. Not established as active. |
| `pi-simple-team` | Idle RPC children stay alive until team shutdown. Logs retain up to 1,000 entries per live team, with full payloads. | Neither live teams nor their child processes automatically return when the main session resumes. |
| Timestamp extension | Notifications add non-persisted transcript components during use. Pi only replaces consecutive status messages at the transcript tail. | Interleaved messages leave older status components behind. Reopening the session removes these components. Magnitude unmeasured. |
| Custom footer | Scans the complete session branch on every render. | Increases resize cost, but the same saved branch restores this cost. |
| Pretty Bash | Reprocesses highlighted output on every render. | Adds rendering work. The audit ruled out accumulating wrapper functions in current Pi. |
| Vanilla Pi | Transcript components rewrap when width changes, including content outside the visible viewport. | Proved size-dependent cost. No indefinite idle-memory growth demonstrated. |

Source locations:

1. [Widget timer and completed snapshots](../../widget.ts#L78), [full preview rendering](../../agent-viewer.ts#L110), [result exchange construction](../../transcript.ts#L132), [child event copies](../../runner.ts#L748).
2. [Simple-team stderr](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/index.ts:419), [animation cleanup](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/render-support/text.ts:129), [bounded team log](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/teamlog.ts:138).
3. [Timestamp notifications](/Users/giladbarnea/.pi/agent/npm/node_modules/@hk_net/pi-timestamp/timestamp.ts:218), [Pi notification routing](/opt/homebrew/lib/node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/dist/modes/interactive/interactive-mode.js:2146), [Pi status retention](/opt/homebrew/lib/node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/dist/modes/interactive/interactive-mode.js:2878).
4. [Custom footer](/Users/giladbarnea/.pi/agent/extensions/custom-footer/index.ts:426), [Pretty Bash](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-pretty-bash/index.ts:94).

Other audited paths provide counterevidence. Current pi-subagents expires completed sessions after ten minutes and caps tombstones. Simple-team removes shut-down teams and clears its dashboard timer. Pi TUI width and image-metadata caches have count limits. Herdr graphics code has explicit replacement/removal cleanup. None of these observations proves absence of another leak.

## Reproducible measurements separate work from retention

The extension baseline passed **226 tests, zero failures**. The following synthetic benchmarks made no model calls and did not alter live sessions.

| Experiment | Result |
|---|---|
| Idle user-agent widget | 10 render requests in 1.1 seconds |

**The restart points to accumulated runtime state, but does not yet prove a memory leak.**

The strongest finding is that **herdr discards old terminal scrollback when it resumes Pi**. Your conversations returned, but that accumulated history did not. Herdr reflows retained history during resizing, including background panes during sidebar changes.

The extension audit found additional suspects:

1. **pi-user-agents:** idle widgets still request 10 renders per second. Long previews can make each render expensive. Restart removes these widgets and live SDK children.
2. **pi-simple-team:** retains unlimited RPC stderr. Idle child processes also remain alive until shutdown. Its animation leak requires an option absent from your global settings.
3. **Other extensions:** timestamp notifications accumulate unsaved transcript components. The custom footer repeatedly scans the complete session history.
4. **Vanilla Pi:** resizing long transcripts is expensive, but short controlled checks showed no sustained heap growth.

I saved the [full findings and measurements](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-user-agents/diagnostics/2026-09-05/findings.md), plus a healthy-state baseline and capture script.

**The next decisive evidence is a CPU and memory capture while it is slow, before restarting.** That can distinguish herdr history processing from Pi rendering or retained child processes.

All 226 baseline tests passed. No extension implementation or settings changed.

content.text:
1. **pi-user-agents: yes, the below-editor widget.**

   Its timer requests a redraw every **100 ms**, even when every agent is idle or finished.

   Each displayed preview also formats the **whole response as Markdown**, then truncates it to one visible line. That repeats even when the response is unchanged.

   We can stop periodic redraws when no agent is active and reuse unchanged previews. The widget would keep the same appearance and controls.

2. **pi-simple-team: stderr is a child process’s diagnostic output.**

   Each RPC child has a separate output stream for warnings, errors, and debug logs. The parent collects that stream like this:

   ```ts
   teammate.stderr += chunk;
   ```

   That string has no size limit. More significantly, **nothing reads it**. The parent keeps every diagnostic character until it releases the teammate object.

   This consumes parent-process memory in proportion to diagnostic output. A quiet child contributes little. A noisy child can contribute much more.

   The **animation leak** is separate. An optional feature makes pending tool indicators blink. It registers a redraw callback for each pending tool.

   When the tool finishes, one return path skips callback removal. A timer still calls those callbacks every **450 ms**, retaining their associated objects.

   Completed tools therefore continue to cause redraw work. The feature defaults to disabled, so we have not established that it affects your sessions.

3. **Timestamp notifications become additional objects in Pi’s displayed conversation.**

   These are the visible lines such as:

   ```text
   Sent 11:03:24
   Done at 11:04:10 · 46s
   ```

   Pi keeps objects for these lines so you can scroll back to them. Interleaved conversation messages prevent older notification lines from being replaced.

   “Unsaved” means **they exist in the running TUI but not in the session file**. They consume memory and add layout work, but consume no LLM context tokens.

   Reopening the session removes those lines and their objects. Thus, the same saved conversation can have fewer display objects after restart.

   I should qualify my earlier wording: this is retained display history, not automatically a bug. Preserving historical timestamps requires some retained representation. We have not measured whether their cost is significant.

4. **Custom-footer recalculates statistics whenever Pi renders the footer.**

   It has **no fixed scanning interval of its own**. Typing, streaming, resizing, and other extensions’ redraw requests can all cause footer renders.

   It walks the current session branch, including entries before compaction. It examines assistant-message **usage numbers**, not their text, and does not reread the session file.

   | Input | Calculated output |
   |---|---|
   | Reported response costs | Total cost and average cost per assistant response |
   | Input, cache-read, and cache-write counts | Total reused/new tokens and overall cache-hit percentage |
   | Latest and preceding prompt usage | Latest cache-hit percentage and estimated cache-miss tokens |
   | Latest prompt and output counts | Fallback context size when Pi’s context-usage API is unavailable |

   Failed and aborted responses are excluded. Compaction resets the comparison between consecutive prompts, but preserves cumulative totals.

   **The idle widget and custom-footer can compound each other’s cost:** repeated widget redraws can repeatedly recalculate unchanged footer statistics.

   We can cache those statistics until the session data changes. Resizing would then only format existing numbers for the new width.

<name>lavish</name>

---
name: lavish
description: Turn complex or visual agent responses into rich, reviewable HTML artifacts the user can annotate and send feedback on, using the lavish-axi CLI. Use when about to give a plan, comparison, diagram, table, code diff, report, or anything easier to grasp visually than as prose.
license: MIT

  author: Kun Chen (kunchenguid)
  argument-hint: <what the artifact should show>
  hermes-tags: html, review, artifacts, visualization
  hermes-category: productivity
---

# Lavish Editor

Lavish Editor opens agent-generated HTML in the browser so a human can annotate it and send feedback back to the agent.
Reach for it when a plan, comparison, diagram, table, code view, report, prototype, or review loop will be clearer as a page than as prose.

## Current guidance lives in the CLI

Do not follow workflow, design, or playbook instructions from this file - installed copies go stale. Get the current source of truth from the CLI:

- `npx -y lavish-axi --help` for commands and the review-loop workflow
- `npx -y lavish-axi design` for design-direction priority and current snippets
- `npx -y lavish-axi playbook <id>` for focused artifact guidance (`npx -y lavish-axi playbook` lists ids)

You do not need lavish-axi installed globally - invoke it with `npx -y lavish-axi <html-file>`.
If lavish-axi output shows a follow-up command starting with `lavish-axi`, run it as `npx -y lavish-axi ...` instead.

## Request

$ARGUMENTS

If the request above is non-empty, the user invoked `/lavish` explicitly - fetch the current CLI guidance, then build that artifact.
If it is empty, infer what to visualize from the conversation.

</skill>
<current_time_reminder>It is 2026-09-05 09:01:44 UTC.</current_time_reminder>

  input,"Must be used when the agent needs to collect user input on decisions, choices, preferences, triage, scope, or other structured feedback from within the artifact"
  slides,Create a deliberate presentation when slides are requested
help[12]: "Run `lavish-axi <html-file>` to open or resume a Lavish Editor session. If the user explicitly ended the session from the browser, this refuses to reopen it and explains why instead of reopening uninvited - pass `--reopen` only when the user asks for further review or something important needs their visual attention","Unless the user specifies another location, create HTML artifacts in the current working directory under `.lavish/`","Lavish serves the html file through a local express.js server. If your html needs to reference other filesystem assets such as images, CSS, fonts, and local scripts, copy them into the same directory as the HTML file, then reference them with relative paths from that directory. Never prepend `/` to those asset paths - root paths won't work","Run `lavish-axi poll <html-file>` to wait for user feedback or browser-proven severe layout failures. It long-polls and stays silent until the user sends feedback, ends the session, or the real browser proves meaningful content is inaccessible or unusable, so leave it running - never kill it. Repair and re-check every returned layout failure before involving the human; cosmetic, intentional, transient, tiny, and uncertain observations stay silent. Keep the poll in the foreground by default and let it return the feedback directly to the agent. A background poll is allowed only through a harness-native tracked background-job facility whose completion result is guaranteed to resume or notify the same agent. Never use `nohup`, shell `&`, `disown`, redirected fire-and-forget processes, or a detached terminal without an explicit verified callback merely to keep polling alive. If the harness has no completion-aware background facility, use the foreground poll or first wire a verified wake callback into the surrounding supervisor. Do not tell the user the artifact is being monitored until that wake path is live. If the poll gets killed or times out anyway, just re-run it - queued feedback is never lost. Codex detected: completed background tasks may not resume Codex automatically, so keep the poll attached to the active turn. `Send & End` ends the session. Its final feedback is still delivered once. After that response, polling stops, and the agent must not reopen the session uninvited.","Rendered Mermaid diagrams in `.mermaid` containers become embedded, editable Excalidraw whiteboards in the browser (click a diagram to unlock editing; a Fullscreen action opens it over the whole viewport) - flowchart, sequence, class, ER, and state diagrams convert to editable shapes; other types embed as an image to draw on. Scenes autosave locally; when a reload detects a changed Mermaid source, the reviewer explicitly chooses to re-convert and discard saved edits or keep editing the saved scene. Standalone and exported copies still render plain Mermaid. Queue feedback adds a prompt to the Conversation panel; when the user sends it, poll returns a tag \"whiteboard\" prompt carrying a bounded edit summary plus local scenePath (.excalidraw JSON) and previewPath (PNG) files - read the summary first, open the files only when needed, then apply the edits by updating the Mermaid source in the artifact (never try to write the scene back)","Run `lavish-axi end <html-file>` to end a session as the agent - ending it this way still allows a plain reopen later. When the user ends it from the browser instead, a later `lavish-axi <html-file>` refuses to reopen it without `--reopen`","Run `lavish-axi export <html-file> [--out <path>]` to write a portable copy of the artifact - one HTML file with its LOCAL assets inlined - so it opens with no Lavish server and no sibling files. Remote CDN/font references are left as links, so it needs network to render those. Users can also export from the browser chrome's overflow menu","Run `lavish-axi share <html-file> [--password <pw>] [--token <t>]` to publish the artifact on ht-ml.app (https://ht-ml.app), a third-party hosting service not part of Lavish, and get back a visitable URL. Shares are PUBLIC by default, so anyone with the link can open them. Pass --password to publish a PRIVATE password-protected page; viewers must supply the password to view. Local assets are inlined; remote refs load over the network. It returns the url plus a secret update_key for managing the page later. Use --token or LAVISH_AXI_HTML_APP_TOKEN only when you have an optional bearer token; it is never required. Users can also publish from the browser chrome's overflow menu",Run `lavish-axi stop` to shut down the background server (it also self-stops when idle or after the last session ends with nothing connected),"Run `lavish-axi playbook <playbook_id>` for focused artifact guidance. One artifact often combines several playbooks (for example a plan that includes a comparison and a diagram), so MUST open each matching playbook before writing HTML.","Lavish does not auto-inject any design system - artifacts stay portable so they render identically when opened directly without lavish-axi running. Before writing any HTML: Decide the design direction in this strict priority order, and only move to the next step when the current one truly yields nothing: (1) if the user asked for a specific look or named design system, use that; (2) otherwise you must first inspect the project the artifact is about - the subject or product whose content or UI it represents, which may differ from your current working directory - and match that project's design system: Tailwind or theme config, shared CSS variables or design tokens, component library, brand assets, or existing styled pages. If the artifact previews, proposes, or mocks a specific app's UI, render it in that app's own design system so it faithfully shows the product, even when you are running in a different repo; (3) only when both steps come up empty, use the Lavish-recommended Tailwind CSS browser runtime v4 + DaisyUI v5, available via CDN, and prefer that CDN snippet over hand-writing styles unless explicitly instructed otherwise by the user. Run `lavish-axi design` for a content-to-playbook router, a copy-pasteable CDN snippet, a Mermaid CDN snippet/init for diagrams, and the DaisyUI component reference. When you deliver the artifact, state which of the three design sources you used and why.","Use lavish-axi when the user asks for a visual artifact, HTML explainer, interactive prototype, review surface, product or technical plan, comparison, report, or browser-based feedback loop"

text(await tools.exec_command({cmd:"mkdir -p .lavish; cat > .lavish/four-extension-costs.html <<'EOF' Four Pi extensions · What the costs mean

Pi performance investigation

Four extensions.
What the costs mean.

1 · User agents2 · Simple team3 · Timestamp4 · Custom footer

01pi-user-agents: yes, the below-editor widget.

Its timer requests a redraw every 100 ms, even when every agent is idle or finished.

Each displayed preview also formats the whole response as Markdown, then truncates it to one visible line. That repeats even when the response is unchanged.

We can stop periodic redraws when no agent is active and reuse unchanged previews. The widget would keep the same appearance and controls.

02pi-simple-team: stderr is a child process’s diagnostic output.

Each RPC child has a separate output stream for warnings, errors, and debug logs. The parent collects that stream like this:

That string has no size limit. More significantly, nothing reads it. The parent keeps every diagnostic character until it releases the teammate object.

This consumes parent-process memory in proportion to diagnostic output. A quiet child contributes little. A noisy child can contribute much more.

The animation leak is separate. An optional feature makes pending tool indicators blink. It registers a redraw callback for each pending tool.

When the tool finishes, one return path skips callback removal. A timer still calls those callbacks every 450 ms, retaining their associated objects.

Completed tools therefore continue to cause redraw work. The feature defaults to disabled, so we have not established that it affects your sessions.

03Timestamp notifications become additional objects in Pi’s displayed conversation.

These are the visible lines such as:

Sent 11:03:24
Done at 11:04:10 · 46s

Pi keeps objects for these lines so you can scroll back to them. Interleaved conversation messages prevent older notification lines from being replaced.

“Unsaved” means they exist in the running TUI but not in the session file. They consume memory and add layout work, but consume no LLM context tokens.

Reopening the session removes those lines and their objects. Thus, the same saved conversation can have fewer display objects after restart.

I should qualify my earlier wording: this is retained display history, not automatically a bug. Preserving historical timestamps requires some retained representation. We have not measured whether their cost is significant.

04Custom-footer recalculates statistics whenever Pi renders the footer.

It has no fixed scanning interval of its own. Typing, streaming, resizing, and other extensions’ redraw requests can all cause footer renders.

It walks the current session branch, including entries before compaction. It examines assistant-message usage numbers, not their text, and does not reread the session file.

InputCalculated output
Reported response costsTotal cost and average cost per assistant response
Input, cache-read, and cache-write countsTotal reused/new tokens and overall cache-hit percentage
Latest and preceding prompt usageLatest cache-hit percentage and estimated cache-miss tokens
Latest prompt and output countsFallback context size when Pi’s context-usage API is unavailable

Failed and aborted responses are excluded. Compaction resets the comparison between consecutive prompts, but preserves cumulative totals.

The idle widget and custom-footer can compound each other’s cost: repeated widget redraws can repeatedly recalculate unchanged footer statistics.

We can cache those statistics until the session data changes. Resizing would then only format existing numbers for the new width.

EOF npx -y lavish-axi .lavish/four-extension-costs.html","max_output_tokens":2000}));

**Red text in `teamlog` does not establish stderr traffic.** Failed tool results reach the parent through HTTP callbacks. The renderer colors their error reason red. Delivery errors also appear red. Actual process stderr appears as an explicitly labeled `stderr` row with a warning icon and muted text. The full stderr buffer is separate from that row’s shortened preview. See [child-tools.ts:174](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/child-tools.ts:174), [render.ts:469](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/render.ts:469), [render.ts:548](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/render.ts:548), and [index.ts:417](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/index.ts:417).

**A completed turn does not release the teammate object or stop its process.** The process stays ready for another message in the same session. That preserves its conversation and permits immediate follow-up work. An unexpected process exit also leaves its teammate object available for resume. `team_shutdown` stops the team’s processes, preserves their durable sessions, and removes the team from the runtime map. Parent session shutdown calls the same cleanup. See [index.ts:423](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/index.ts:423), [index.ts:571](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/index.ts:571), and [index.ts:867](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/index.ts:867).

Removing the team releases its main runtime reference. Garbage collection can reclaim the teammate objects after pending callbacks and deliveries also release their references. Therefore, “freed immediately at shutdown” would be too strong. The unused stderr buffer remains attached until that point. No buffer reset occurs between turns or teammate resumes.

**The pending indicator belongs to tool calls in the main Pi transcript.** It is the bullet beside an executing `team_spawn`, `team_list`, `team_resume`, `team_add`, `teamsend`, `teamstatus`, `teamlog`, `team_shutdown`, or `schedule_reminder` call. It is not the `/team` dashboard refresh or a teammate status indicator. Normal child runtimes do not register these custom tool renderers. Overseeing teammates do. See [render.ts:846](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/render.ts:846), [render.ts:873](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/render.ts:873), and [index.ts:850](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/index.ts:850).

**When animation is disabled throughout the runtime, this feature starts no timer and causes no periodic redraw.** Its disabled branch clears any matching tracked entry and returns a static warning-colored bullet. Only the enabled branch starts the 450ms timer. The default is disabled. See [text.ts:170](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/render-support/text.ts:170) and [settings.ts:158](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/render-support/settings.ts:158).

The confirmed defect applies after animation actually starts: completion bypasses cleanup, so the timer continues calling the retained tool’s `context.invalidate()`. That requests further rendering through Pi. It is not a disabled-feature timer. See [text.ts:136](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/render-support/text.ts:136) and [text.ts:183](/Users/giladbarnea/dev/pi-extensions/pi-simple-team/render-support/text.ts:183).

The pi-simple-team check clarifies two points:

With animation disabled, **no animation timer starts**. The leak requires animation to have been enabled first.

Actual stderr appears in a labeled `stderr` row. Red text can instead come from failed tools or message delivery. I will add these distinctions to Lavish.

playbook:
  id: input
  use_when: "Must be used when the agent needs to collect user input on decisions, choices, preferences, triage, scope, or other structured feedback from within the artifact"
  choose[3]: "Use this when the user needs to select, tune, triage, annotate, or edit a structured choice.",Use controls for decisions the user can make faster visually than by writing a prompt.,Use plain annotations when the artifact only needs open-ended feedback.
  structure[4]: "Make each decision surface visible: what is being chosen, what the options mean, and what happens next.",Keep reversible selection state local in the artifact until the user explicitly submits that question.,Pair each question with a Submit or Queue answer control that sends exactly one prompt for the final answer.,Show selected state separately from queued state so the user trusts what will be sent back.
  design_rules[9]: "Native controls - radios, checkboxes, text inputs, selects, textareas, buttons, options, labels, disclosure summaries, and contenteditable regions - are interactive automatically: clicks toggle, focus, and type instead of annotating, so they do not need data-lavish-action. Build choice and option UIs from these whenever you can.","For reversible choices, do not call window.lavish.queuePrompt() from radio change handlers or option click handlers. Those handlers should only update local selected state.",Use a per-question form submit or explicit Queue answer button to read the current values and call window.lavish.queuePrompt() exactly once for the final answer.,Put data-lavish-action only on custom (non-native) elements that should act like a feedback control - typically a styled div or span you made clickable - so Lavish does not annotate it and shows a pointer cursor instead.,Use data-lavish-question on a question wrapper or pass queueKey when multiple pre-send updates should replace the prior unsent answer for the same question.,"Pass options such as tag, text, selector, target, data, queueKey, or element when they help the agent understand exactly what the user chose.",Call window.lavish.sendQueuedPrompts() only when the control should immediately send committed feedback instead of waiting for the user to press Send to Agent.,Make queued prompts specific enough that the agent can act without asking a follow-up question.,Keep native browser controls accessible and readable on mobile.
  pitfalls[4]: "Do not queue one prompt per radio change, checkbox toggle, dropdown change, or choice-button click when the user can still change their mind.",Do not create controls whose queued prompt is unclear or too vague to execute.,Do not hide the difference between selected locally and queued for the agent.,Do not require interaction for content the user only needs to read.
  lavish_notes[5]: Lavish is strongest when the artifact becomes a focused review surface and not just a static page.,"A native single-choice question should submit the final value: `<form data-lavish-question=\"plan\" onsubmit=\"event.preventDefault(); const choice = new FormData(event.currentTarget).get('plan'); if (choice) window.lavish.queuePrompt('Use the ' + choice + ' plan', { tag: 'choice', text: 'Plan: ' + choice, element: event.currentTarget, data: { question: 'plan', answer: choice } });\"><label><input type=\"radio\" name=\"plan\" value=\"Starter\"> Starter</label><label><input type=\"radio\" name=\"plan\" value=\"Pro\"> Pro</label><button type=\"submit\">Queue this answer</button></form>`.","A custom choice UI should make option buttons update local state, then use a separate Queue answer button with data-lavish-action to queue the final selected value.","Use window.lavish.queuePrompt for user intent, not internal analytics or UI-only state changes.",End input paths with an obvious way for the user to send feedback back to the agent.
playbook:
  id: comparison
  use_when: "Show options, tradeoffs, and current vs target behavior"
  choose[3]: Use before and after when the same system is changing over time.,Use option cards when the user needs to choose between mutually exclusive directions.,Use a scorecard only when the criteria are explicit and comparable.
  structure[3]: Name the decision at the top of the artifact.,"Show the concrete behavior or artifact shape for each side, not just abstract pros and cons.",End with a recommendation only when the evidence actually supports one.
  design_rules[3]: Keep corresponding details aligned so differences are visible without hunting.,Use visual hierarchy to separate primary tradeoffs from secondary notes.,Make the cost of each option as visible as the benefit.
  pitfalls[3]: Do not make every option look equally recommended if one is clearly preferred.,Do not compare vague summaries when concrete examples are available.,Do not bury assumptions that would change the recommendation.
  lavish_notes[2]: A Lavish comparison should let the user annotate the exact option or tradeoff they want changed.,"If the goal is selection, provide controls that queue the chosen option with rationale."

  design_rules[9]: "Native controls - radios, checkboxes, text inputs, selects, textareas, buttons, options, labels, disclosure summaries, and contenteditable regions - are interactive automatically: clicks toggle, focus, and type instead of annotating, so they do not need data-lavish-action. Build choice and option UIs from these whenever you can.","For reversible choices, do not call window.lavish.queuePrompt() from radio change handlers or option click handlers. Those handlers should only update local selected state.",Use a per-question form submit or explicit Queue answer button to read the current values and call window.lavish.queuePrompt() exactly once for the final answer.,Put data-lavish-action only on custom (non-native) elements that should act like a feedback control - typically a styled div or span you made clickable - so Lavish does not annotate it and shows a pointer cursor instead.,Use data-lavish-question on a question wrapper or pass queueKey when multiple pre-send updates should replace the prior unsent answer for the same question.,"Pass options such as tag, text, selector, target, data, queueKey, or element when they help the agent understand exactly what the user chose.",Call window.lavish.sendQueuedPrompts() only when the control should immediately send committed feedback instead of waiting for the user to press Send to Agent.,Make queued prompts specific enough that the agent can act without asking a follow-up question.,Keep native browser controls accessible and readable on mobile.
  pitfalls[4]: "Do not queue one prompt per radio change, checkbox toggle, dropdown change, or choice-button click when the user can still change their mind.",Do not create controls whose queued prompt is unclear or too vague to execute.,Do not hide the difference between selected locally and queued for the agent.,Do not require interaction for content the user only needs to read.
  lavish_notes[5]: Lavish is strongest when the artifact becomes a focused review surface and not just a static page.,"A native single-choice question should submit the final value: `<form data-lavish-question=\"plan\" onsubmit=\"event.preventDefault(); const choice = new FormData(event.currentTarget).get('plan'); if (choice) window.lavish.queuePrompt('Use the ' + choice + ' plan', { tag: 'choice', text: 'Plan: ' + choice, element: event.currentTarget, data: { question: 'plan', answer: choice } });\"><label><input type=\"radio\" name=\"plan\" value=\"Starter\"> Starter</label><label><input type=\"radio\" name=\"plan\" value=\"Pro\"> Pro</label><button type=\"submit\">Queue this answer</button></form>`.","A custom choice UI should make option buttons update local state, then use a separate Queue answer button with data-lavish-action to queue the final selected value.","Use window.lavish.queuePrompt for user intent, not internal analytics or UI-only state changes.",End input paths with an obvious way for the user to send feedback back to the agent.
playbook:
  id: comparison
  use_when: "Show options, tradeoffs, and current vs target behavior"
  choose[3]: Use before and after when the same system is changing over time.,Use option cards when the user needs to choose between mutually exclusive directions.,Use a scorecard only when the criteria are explicit and comparable.
  structure[3]: Name the decision at the top of the artifact.,"Show the concrete behavior or artifact shape for each side, not just abstract pros and cons.",End with a recommendation only when the evidence actually supports one.
  design_rules[3]: Keep corresponding details aligned so differences are visible without hunting.,Use visual hierarchy to separate primary tradeoffs from secondary notes.,Make the cost of each option as visible as the benefit.
  pitfalls[3]: Do not make every option look equally recommended if one is clearly preferred.,Do not compare vague summaries when concrete examples are available.,Do not bury assumptions that would change the recommendation.
  lavish_notes[2]: A Lavish comparison should let the user annotate the exact option or tradeoff they want changed.,"If the goal is selection, provide controls that queue the chosen option with rationale."

**Three separate history scans affect Custom Footer.** Only two run during resize. The skill scan runs on session events.

| Displayed item | Actual dependency and work | Estimated severity |
|---|---|---|
| Context gauge, percentage, used/window tokens | Each footer render calls `getContextUsage()`. Pi reconstructs the complete branch, finds the latest compaction, checks valid usage, then estimates trailing messages. | High during resize |
| Total cost, average cost/turn, session cache hit, latest cache hit/miss, reused/new totals | All share **one** `getSessionStats()` pass per footer render. It reconstructs the complete branch, then reads assistant usage fields and performs arithmetic. | High during resize, shared cost |
| Session name above the editor | Each header render calls `getSessionName()`. Pi filters **all session entries** into a new array, then searches backward for the latest name. | High during resize for large session trees |
| Skill names and token ages above the editor | Refresh calls `getContextUsage()`, rebuilds effective history, enumerates commands, scans history twice, searches user text, and compares each read path against every skill path. Rendering uses saved names and ages. | High refresh work; low resize work |
| Context gradient colors | Each footer render formats four theme colors, parses their ANSI codes, then interpolates RGB values. | Low, fixed work |
| Git branch, dirty marker, directory | Rendering reads saved values. Session start, turn end, and Git branch changes run Git commands. | Low resize work; separate event-driven subprocess work |

These are estimates from the call stack, not timing results. “High” identifies history-dependent work inside frequent rendering.

Important dependency details:

1. **Removing one cache label does not remove the shared scan.** Cost totals, cache figures, and fallback context tokens come from the same function.

4. **The model and thinking labels are inexpensive.** The session-name lookup causes the header’s history-dependent work.
5. **Token estimation is not tokenization.** Pi reads text lengths and content blocks. It serializes assistant tool-call arguments only when estimating those messages.
6. **Extension status rendering has a separate disk operation.** It serializes statuses every render and calls `appendFileSync` when statuses change.

Pi performance investigation

Four extensions.
What the costs mean.

1 · User agents2 · Simple team3 · Timestamp4 · Custom footer

01pi-user-agents · approved changes

Implemented · 230 tests passed

  1. Stop periodic redraws when all agents are idle.
  2. Reuse unchanged previews.
  3. Truncate the text before Markdown rendering.
  4. Use a 200 ms periodic redraw interval while agents are active.
  5. Remove turn-completion cards from the main transcript, including old cards on reload.

The below-editor widget and agent overlay stay available. Squash still delivers the full exchange to the main agent. Completion cards are the separate objects you asked to remove.

All 230 pi-user-agents tests passed. The widget, overlay, child session files, and hidden squash delivery remain available. Existing Pi processes need an extension reload or restart to use the edits.

02pi-simple-team · your questions

The full stderr string is unused, but incoming stderr does also feed log previews. My earlier explanation did not make that distinction clear enough.

Each incoming chunk is appended to the full string. A shortened preview also appears in an explicitly labeled stderr log row. The full string is not read back to create that row.

Red text alone does not identify stderr. Failed tool results and message-delivery errors can appear red. A labeled stderr row identifies process diagnostic output.

A finished turn does not stop or release a teammate. Its Pi process stays ready for another message in the same session. This preserves its conversation and avoids process startup and session reload for each follow-up.

An unexpected process exit also leaves its teammate object available for resume. The accumulated stderr string remains attached across turns and resumes.

team_shutdown stops the team’s processes and removes the team from the runtime map. Parent session shutdown uses the same cleanup. Session files remain on disk.

“Release” means removing references to the objects. Garbage collection can reclaim them after pending callbacks and deliveries also drop their references. It does not mean memory necessarily returns to the operating system immediately.

Pending-tool animation has been removed. You never requested this feature. Disabling it is not the intended solution.

Pending tools now use a static indicator. The animation setting, conditional branch, timer, callback map, and animation-only helpers are deleted.

Removed · 72 render tests passed

03Timestamp · out of scope

You want to keep the timestamp lines. No timestamp changes.

04Custom-footer · cost map before changes

These rankings come from the call stack and operations, not timing measurements. “High” means history-dependent work inside frequent rendering. It does not claim a measured delay.

The lower footer performs two separate history scans per render. The session-name header adds an independent scan. Skill discovery scans history on session events, but uses cached results during resize.

Displayed itemWork on each redrawEstimated cost
Context gauge, percentage, used/window tokensPi builds the full branch, finds compaction and usage boundaries, then estimates trailing messages.High: depends on history and trailing content.
Total cost, average cost/turn, all cache figuresOne shared full-branch pass reads assistant usage numbers and calculates totals and ratios.High: depends on branch length.
Session name above the editorPi filters all session entries into a new array, then searches backward for the latest name.High for large session trees.
Skill names and token agesFormats saved names and ages. Discovery runs on session start, turn end, compaction, and tree changes.Low during resize. High during refresh.
Context gradient colorsParses four theme colors and blends RGB values.Low: fixed work.
Model, thinking level, Git branch, directoryFormats current or saved values. Git commands run on separate events.Low during resize.
Other extensions’ status linesSerializes statuses. Writes a log synchronously only when statuses change.Small with few statuses; conditional disk I/O.

Removing one cache label does not remove its shared scan. Total cost, average cost, cache totals, cache ratios, and fallback context tokens come from the same calculation. Narrow mode still calculates the hidden fields.

Context token estimation does not tokenize text. It reads text lengths and content blocks. It can serialize tool-call arguments when estimating trailing assistant messages.

Skill refresh rebuilds effective history, enumerates installed skills, searches messages for loads, and matches read paths against skill paths. Removing only the age label would leave skill discovery intact.

My recommendation: cache the shared statistics, context usage, and session name until their inputs change. Choose removals for information you no longer value, rather than removing one cheap label while leaving its shared scan.

The footer is unchanged while you review this map.

Choose the footer scope

The full stderr string is unused, but incoming stderr does also feed log previews. My earlier explanation did not make that distinction clear enough.

Each incoming chunk is appended to the full string. A shortened preview also appears in an explicitly labeled stderr log row. The full string is not read back to create that row.

Red text alone does not identify stderr. Failed tool results and message-delivery errors can appear red. A labeled stderr row identifies process diagnostic output.

A finished turn does not stop or release a teammate. Its Pi process stays ready for another message in the same session. This preserves its conversation and avoids process startup and session reload for each follow-up.

An unexpected process exit also leaves its teammate object available for resume. The accumulated stderr string remains attached across turns and resumes.

team_shutdown stops the team’s processes and removes the team from the runtime map. Parent session shutdown uses the same cleanup. Session files remain on disk.

“Release” means removing references to the objects. Garbage collection can reclaim them after pending callbacks and deliveries also drop their references. It does not mean memory necessarily returns to the operating system immediately.

With animation disabled from the start, no animation timer starts. There is no periodic no-op timer and no 450 ms redraw tax from this feature.

The optional animation controls the bullet beside executing tools in the main Pi transcript: team_spawn, team_list, team_resume, team_add, teamsend, teamstatus, teamlog, team_shutdown, and schedule_reminder.

Animation stateTimer behavior
Disabled throughout runtimeNo animation timer or periodic redraw.
Enabled while a tool runsTimer invalidates the tool view every 450 ms.
Tool completes after animation startedBug: cleanup is skipped. The callback stays retained and continues to request rendering.

The feature defaults to disabled. That means the code does not wrongly assume it is enabled. The confirmed leak applies only after animation actually starts.

Session name above the editorPi filters all session entries into a new array, then searches backward for the latest name.High for large session trees.
Skill names and token agesFormats saved names and ages. Discovery runs on session start, turn end, compaction, and tree changes.Low during resize. High during refresh.
Context gradient colorsParses four theme colors and blends RGB values.Low: fixed work.

Skill refresh rebuilds effective history, enumerates installed skills, searches messages for loads, and matches read paths against skill paths. Removing only the age label would leave skill discovery intact.

Four extensions.
Changes and choices.

1 · User agents2 · Simple team3 · Timestamp4 · Custom footer

01pi-user-agents · done

230 tests passed

  • No periodic redraws while idle. Active agents refresh every 200 ms.
  • Previews truncate before Markdown rendering and reuse unchanged results.
  • Completion cards no longer appear in the main transcript.

The below-editor widget, overlay, and squash still work.

Reload the extension or restart Pi to use these changes.

02pi-simple-team · animation removed

72 render tests passed

Pending tools now use a static indicator. The animation setting, timer, callbacks, and branches are deleted.

Stderr still needs attention. The parent keeps an unlimited diagnostic string that nothing reads. Log previews come directly from incoming chunks, not that stored string.

Look for a labeled stderr row. Red text can also mean a failed tool or message delivery.

Teammates stay alive between turns to preserve their conversation and accept follow-ups without restarting. Their stderr stays in memory too.

03Timestamp · keep as is

No changes, as requested.

04Custom-footer · choose what to keep

Three history scans repeat during redraws: context usage, cost/cache statistics, and the session name.

Estimates below come from the code, without timing tests. “High” means the work grows with session history.

DisplayRepeated workEstimated cost
Context gauge and token countsScans history and estimates trailing messages.High
Cost and cache figuresShares one history scan for totals and ratios.High
Session nameSearches all session entries.High
Skill names and agesReuses saved results during redraws. Refresh scans history on session events.Low redraw cost; high refresh cost
Colors, model, thinking, Git, directoryFormats current or saved values.Low redraw cost
Extension status linesFormats statuses. Writes a log when they change.Usually small; includes disk writes

Removing one cache label saves little. The remaining cost/cache labels still need the shared scan. Narrow mode also computes hidden figures.

No footer changes yet.

Choose an option, then queue your decision.

04Custom-footer · one shared cache

Your question: Can we keep every display, extract the data together, and cache it?

Yes to keeping every display and sharing cached data. Each display would read the same saved results. Resizing and typing would not scan history again.

One correction: cost totals and cache figures already share a single scan. The repeated work comes from recalculating them on every redraw, plus separate context-usage and session-name lookups.

  1. Calculate all cost and cache figures together when conversation data changes.
  2. Refresh context usage when messages, compaction, or the model change.
  3. Refresh the session name when it changes or another session opens.
  4. Keep skill discovery outside rendering and reuse its saved results.

Literally one scan for every value would require more changes. Pi’s context-usage API and skill discovery have their own history rules. Combining those into one pass would mean replacing existing logic.

I recommend one shared cache, not a rewrite of Pi’s history logic. Run each needed calculation only when its inputs change. The redraw path then does no history scans.

All displays stay. This is the design answer; the footer implementation is still unchanged.

We can keep every display and share cached results, with no history scans during redraws. A literal single pass for every value would require replacing Pi context logic, so I recommend caching the existing calculations when their inputs change.'","yield_time_ms":1000,"max_output_tokens":1000}));

# ~/.pi: Pi CLI Coding Agent user configuration directory

“Pi” is a CLI AI agent, similar to Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, etc.

It's open source and highly hackable. Author encourages implementing custom extensions and modifying core behavior per each user’s taste.

Pi ships with local docs, examples and source code, stored here: `/opt/homebrew/lib/node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/`.
Almost all tasks that take place here (`~/.pi`) revolve around improving usability, UX, quality-of-life and ergonomics for me. This means search (with high recall) and fully reading resources in the dir above at session start.

Additionally, there is a qmd `pi-source` collection which encompasses the `docs`, `examples` and `dist` subdirs of the source. Alternate between grepping, qmd-ing, and reading resources.

# Global Instructions

## Ecosystem
You’re on a Mac M2 Pro. In addition to base Unix coreutils and Python 3, you can also leverage the following tools: `rg`, `fd`, `jq`, `yq`, `http`, `uv`, `npx`, `ruff`, and more.

<core-tools>

### Core Tools

<tool-usage>

**1. `rg`**

  Great for searching patterns/regex across a directory or specific files. You can customize the output with its CLI options—for example, show line numbers (`-n`) or list only matching files (`-l`). It’s essentially a drop-in replacement for `grep`, so familiar options like `-C` work too.
  *Bottom line: use `rg [-u]` instead of `grep` and the built-in `Search`.*

**2. `fd`**

  Great for finding files.
  *Bottom line: use `fd` instead of `find`.*

**3. Built-in `read_file` tool**

  *Bottom line: **Always read files in full.***

**4. `FORCE_OMZ=1 /usr/bin/env zsh -ic '...'`**

  If some executables aren’t available in `PATH`, try running the command this way. It automatically sources the user’s `.zshrc`, which loads key environment variables and `PATH` entries, making lots of additional commands and tools available.

**5. `gsd`**

  Stands for git structured diff. `gsd` is a superior drop-in replacement for `git diff` that prints the diff in a structured, ai-agent-friendly format. It categorizes the changes guarantees that you understand the diff completely.

<development-rules>

## Development Rules

<tenets>

### Be Bold, Precise and Minimalistic

1. Fail loud and early.
2. Complexity is the enemy.
3. Simplicity is how good things happen (and last).
4. Adding a logical branch is unjustified unless proven otherwise.
5. No nested `if` statements.
6. Write declarative, upfront code. The more the source code feels like a high-level configuration rather than an implementation, the better. Just like a Pydantic BaseModel definition is easier to understand than a vanilla Python class with an implemented `__init__`, manual value and custom validation, manual state setting, etc.
7. No weasel code. Don’t carry over cascading uncertainty via defensive programming. Be straightforward and explicit.

</tenets>

<principles>

1. Do not abbreviate variable, function or class names. Use complete words. Write clean code.
2. Write code that fails early and clearly. Don’t write fallbacks to “maybe broken” inputs. No “Just in case my inputs are corrupted” code. Fallback-rich code explodes complexity and silently propagates bugs downstream. Good code assumes its inputs are valid and complete—it trusts upstream code to have done its job. This ties closely to separation of concerns. And if something important fails, or an upstream logic failed to fulfil its contract, fail early and clearly. Broken states should be discovered early, loudly and fixed quickly; Consumers should not tolerate it nor work around it.
3. Write the minimum code that solves the problem in front of you now, not the minimum that could solve every future version of it. Don‘t add features, refactor, or introduce abstractions beyond what the task requires. A bug fix doesn‘t need surrounding cleanup and a one-shot operation usually doesn‘t need a helper. Avoid premature abstraction and half-finished implementations. The test: if the only reason something is abstracted is “in case we need to,” you have over-built it. Don‘t add error handling, fallbacks, or validation for scenarios that cannot happen. Trust internal code and framework guarantees. Only validate at system boundaries (user input, external APIs). Don't use feature flags or backwards-compatibility shims when you can just change the code.
4. Write highly cohesive, decoupled logic.
5. Leverage existing logic when possible. Do not re-implement anything.
6. Write flat, optimized logical branches. Avoid nested, duplicate-y code. Write DRY and elegant logic. Push cyclomatic complexity to a minimum. More declariveness, less implementation.
7. Add a doctest example to pure-ish functions (data in, data out).

</principles>

<typing-style>

### Typing Style

The following principles apply to any typed language: Python, TypeScript, Rust, etc.
1. Use modern annotations. <no>`Optional[Dict]`</no>, <yes>`dict | None`</yes>.
2. Parametrize container types until you hit a bottom primitive type. <no>`list`</no>, <yes>`list[int]`</yes>. <no>`dict`</no>, <no>`dict[str, list]`</no>, <yes>`dict[str, list[int]]`</yes>.
3. Type all function arguments, return types and variables, as long as it makes sense.
4. Don’t use `Any`. If you don’t know the type, that’s a smell — make a small effort to discover it what it is empirically, then annotate accordingly.
5. Prefer protocols to concrete types. For example, if a function only iterates over a passed value, annotate the argument as `Iterable[...]` rather than `list[...]`. Duck typing is good.

<core-engineering-philosophy>

## Core Engineering Philosophy

1. Avoid increasing complexity without a truly justified reason. Each new line of code or logical branch costs an increase in complexity. **Complexity is the enemy**. In your decision-making, ask yourself how you might **REDUCE complexity**, rather than just solve the immediate problem ad-hoc. Oftentimes, reducing complexity means **REMOVING code**. If done right, removing code is better than writing a solution because it removes the circumstances that give rise to the problem in the first place. It’s like clearing Tetris blocks — it simplifies and creates more space.
2. Prefer **declarative design** over imperative approaches. From a single variable to an entire system, if you can express it declaratively upfront, do so. Make the full picture visible straight up to allow to understand the system without needing read the implementation. Do not embed flow and rules in sprawling implementation details.
3. Avoid overengineering and excessive abstraction. Abstractions have to be clearly justified. Simplicity and clarity are key.
4. Do not write comments in code unless they are critical for understanding the “why.”
5. Do not fix linter and formatter errors unless instructed to do so.
6. Docstrings should be succinct and direct. 1–2 sentences max of what the function does and its role in its larger calling scope. No need to document arguments and return type: use type annotations for that. Do document if it intentionally raises exceptions.

</core-engineering-philosophy>

## How To Approach a Task

<how-to-approach-a-task>

The following points are close to my heart:
1. **Every task needs a disprovable falsification criterion and a provable success criterion before code is written**. "Add validation" becomes "reject a missing or malformed email, return 400 with a clear message, and test both cases." Break larger tasks down by **which checkpoints have to be _PROVEN_** before you commit to an approach.
2. Figure out exactly what you are doing before you type. State your assumptions: "add authentication" is several different tasks, so name them explicitly. Name the tradeoffs when they matter to the approach. If the scope is truly vague, stop and ask rather than filling the gap with plausible-looking code; that is exactly the code that passes a casual review and fails when it matters. Vague scope is the reason to ask. A clear scope is yours to act on.
3. Before starting your task, you must **understand all the affected code downstream and all the affecting code upstream**. Not only the blast radius, but also whether we’re going to transfer a power plant that a town nearby relies on. Are we going to redirect a water pipe that an adjacent city consumes? How far along the stack does this go? Map out the moving parts and coupling instances before thinking and planning.
4. When something breaks, investigate; do not guess. Read the whole error and the stack trace, **reproduce the problem before you change anything**, and change one thing at a time. If you are fixing a bug, nail down the **root cause** before thinking of a solution. Do not paper over an unexpected `null` with a null check; find out why it is null, or the bug just moves somewhere quieter.
5. When making changes, be absolutely SURGICAL. Every changed line must be justified by the task. Every line of code you add incurs a small debt; this debt compounds over time through increased complexity, maintenance costs, bugs, and cognitive load. Therefore, make only laser-focused changes.

</how-to-approach-a-task>

<being-an-effective-ai-agent>

1. Know your weaknesses: your eagerness to solve a problem can cause tunnel vision. Avoid tunnel-vision failure modes: Don’t fix a problem at the cost of unintentionally breaking something else that was out of your field of view; Don’t deviate from the existing design or from established patterns. Overcome by looking around beyond the immediate fix, be aware of (and account for) coupling around the codebase, integrate with the existing design and periodically refactor.
2. You do your best work when you can verify yourself. With self-verification, you can and should practice continuous trial and error instead of a single shot in the dark.
3. **If the scope is clear, act. Don't ask.** Reversible and cheap? Do it, then tell your human. Research, data pulls, analysis, drafts, refactors inside the scope your human gave you, feasibility tests in a temporary scratchpad, and API tests. A question costs your human more than a re-run costs you. Ask first only for a truly vague scope, anything reaching an audience, anything you cannot undo, or anything expensive. Something is broken? </being-an-effective-ai-agent>

# Global Instructions

## Ecosystem
You’re on a Mac M2 Pro. In addition to base Unix coreutils and Python 3, you can also leverage the following tools: `rg`, `fd`, `jq`, `yq`, `http`, `uv`, `npx`, `ruff`, and more.
